q: Time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
o: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
e:
Binary search looks at the middle element. If the target is smaller, it throws away the right half; if bigger, the left half. Then it repeats on what is left.
Each step halves the remaining items: 1,000,000 → 500,000 → 250,000 ... so it needs only about 20 steps. That is O(log n).
It only works on SORTED data. Python has it in the `bisect` module.
r: Halving each step = O(log n).

q: Average and worst-case lookup in a hash table?
o: O(1) on average, O(n) in the worst case
O(log n) in both the average and worst case
O(1) in both the average and worst case
O(n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case
e:
A hash table (Python dict or set) computes a hash of the key to jump directly to the right slot, so a lookup takes about the same time no matter how big it is: O(1) on average.
If many keys land in the same slot (collisions), it must check them one by one; in the worst case that is O(n). Good hash functions make this very rare.
r: dict/set lookup ≈ O(1).
fa: O(1) average, O(n) worst

q: What is the lower bound for comparison-based sorting?
o: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
e:
A comparison sort only learns about the data by comparing two items ('is a < b?'). It can be proven that, in the worst case, any such algorithm needs about n log n comparisons.
So merge sort, heapsort and Timsort (O(n log n)) are already optimal.
Sorts that do not compare, like counting sort or radix sort, can be O(n) for limited kinds of keys (e.g. small integers).
r: Comparison sorting can't beat O(n log n).

q: Worst case of quicksort, and when does it happen?
o: O(n log n) on average, and never worse on any input
O(n²) when pivots are bad, like a sorted input
O(n) when the input array is already sorted
O(log n) when the pivot is always the median
e:
Quicksort picks a pivot, puts smaller items on its left and larger on its right, then sorts each side.
If the pivot is always the smallest or largest item (e.g. picking the first element of an already sorted list), one side is empty every time, so it does n + (n-1) + ... steps = O(n²).
Random pivots or median-of-three make that extremely unlikely. Python's `sorted` uses Timsort, which is O(n log n) in the worst case.
r: Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) with bad pivots.
fa: O(n²), with consistently bad pivots (e.g. first element on already sorted input)

q: Which is true about merge sort?
o: It sorts in place with O(1) memory, but it is not stable
It is stable, O(n log n) always, and needs O(n) extra space
Its worst case is O(n²) when the input is nearly sorted
It only works on linked lists, never on plain arrays
e:
Merge sort splits the list in halves until single items remain, then merges sorted halves back together. Every level takes O(n) work and there are log n levels: O(n log n), always.
Merging needs a temporary array: O(n) extra memory.
It is stable: equal items keep their original order, which matters when you sort by one field after another.
r: Merge sort = always O(n log n), stable, needs extra memory.
fa: Stable, O(n log n) in all cases, O(n) extra space for arrays

q: Two Sum: find indices of two numbers adding to `target`. Optimal approach?
o: Two nested loops over the array, O(n²)
Sort first, then binary search for each value, O(n log n)
One pass with a hash map from value to index, O(n)
Recursion that tries every pair of numbers
e:
For each number x, the partner we need is `target - x`. Instead of searching the whole list for it (O(n) each time), we keep a dict of numbers already seen and their index.
Check the dict (O(1)); if the partner is there, done; otherwise store x. One pass: O(n).
This trade of memory for speed with a hash map is one of the most common interview tricks.
r: Need 'have I seen X before?' fast → hash map.
fa: One pass with a hash map from value to index, O(n) time, O(n) space

q: Detect a cycle in a linked list with O(1) extra space?
o: Store each visited node in a hash set and look for repeats
Floyd's: a slow and a fast pointer meet when there is a cycle
Reverse the list in place and compare it with the original
Sort the nodes by value and look for any repeated nodes
e:
Use two pointers: the slow one moves 1 node per step, the fast one 2 nodes.
If the list ends, there is no cycle. If there IS a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one inside the loop and they meet, like two runners on a circular track.
A set of visited nodes also works but uses O(n) memory.
r: Cycle detection: fast and slow pointers.
fa: Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; they meet if there is a cycle

q: Shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph?
o: DFS
BFS
Dijkstra with a max-heap
Topological sort
e:
BFS (breadth-first search) explores in rings: first all neighbors 1 step away, then all at 2 steps, and so on, using a queue.
So the first time BFS reaches a node, it got there with the fewest possible edges.
DFS goes deep along one path first, so the first path it finds may be long. Cost of BFS: O(V + E).
r: Fewest steps in an unweighted graph → BFS.

q: Dijkstra's algorithm requires…
o: A directed acyclic graph (DAG)
Edge weights that are not negative
A graph without weights on its edges
An adjacency matrix as the representation
e:
Dijkstra finds shortest paths when edges have weights (distances, costs). It always expands the closest unvisited node next (using a min-heap) and treats its distance as final.
That 'final' decision is only correct if no edge can make a path shorter later, i.e. no negative weights.
With negative weights use Bellman-Ford. Complexity with a heap: O((V + E) log V).
r: Dijkstra = weighted shortest path, no negative edges.
fa: Non-negative edge weights

q: You need an order to install packages given 'A depends on B' relations. Algorithm?
o: Binary search on the list of packages
Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm or DFS) on a DAG
Kruskal's algorithm for a minimum spanning tree
Quickselect on the number of dependencies
e:
Dependencies form a directed graph. A topological sort lists the nodes so every node comes after everything it depends on.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a node with no remaining dependencies (in-degree 0), output it, and remove its edges.
If some nodes are never freed, there is a cycle (circular dependency), and no valid order exists.
r: Order with dependencies → topological sort.

q: Best way to get the k largest elements from a stream of n numbers?
o: Sort all n numbers first: O(n log n)
Keep a min-heap of size k: O(n log k)
Push all n into a max-heap, then pop k
Scan the numbers k times: O(nk) overall
e:
A heap is a structure that always gives you its smallest item in O(1) and adds/removes in O(log size).
Keep a min-heap with the k largest numbers seen so far. For each new number, push it; if the heap has more than k items, pop the smallest.
The heap never grows past k, so the cost is O(n log k), and memory is only O(k). Python: `heapq.nlargest(k, numbers)`.
r: Top k → heap of size k.

q: Longest substring without repeating characters. Optimal technique and complexity?
o: Brute force over all substrings, O(n³)
Sliding window with a last-seen map, O(n)
Sort the characters first, O(n log n)
A DP table over all substring pairs, O(n²)
e:
A sliding window is a range [left, right] over the string that you grow and shrink instead of restarting.
Move `right` forward one character at a time. If that character already appears inside the window, move `left` just past its previous position. Track the best window length.
Each pointer only moves forward, so the total work is O(n).
r: Best contiguous substring/subarray → sliding window.

q: In a sorted array, find whether two numbers sum to target using O(1) space.
o: Hash set of the numbers seen so far (O(n) space)
Two pointers from both ends, moving by the sum
Build a binary search tree from the whole array
Recursively try every pair of numbers in the array
e:
Put one pointer at the start (smallest) and one at the end (largest).
If their sum is too small, move the left pointer right to get a bigger number. If too big, move the right pointer left. If equal, done.
Because the array is sorted, each move safely discards one candidate: O(n) time, no extra memory.
r: Sorted array + pair search → two pointers.
fa: Two pointers from both ends, moving inward based on the sum

q: Which two properties indicate a problem fits dynamic programming?
o: Sorted input and unique values
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Graph input and the presence of cycles
Recursion and some randomness in the choices
e:
Dynamic programming (DP) solves a big problem by combining answers to smaller versions of it, and saves each small answer so it is computed only once.
It fits when:
- Optimal substructure: the best answer is built from best answers of subproblems.
- Overlapping subproblems: the same subproblems come up again and again.
Two styles: top-down with memoization (`@lru_cache`) or bottom-up filling a table.
r: DP = solve subproblems once and reuse them.

q: Time complexity of memoized Fibonacci `fib(n)`?
o: O(2ⁿ)
O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
e:
Naive recursive fib calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), which call the same values again and again: about 2ⁿ calls.
With memoization, each fib(k) is computed once and then read from a cache. There are only n different values, so O(n).
r: Memoization turns repeated work into one-time work.

q: A deep recursive DFS in Python on a 100,000-node path graph will likely…
o: Run fine, since Python optimizes deep recursion
Hit a RecursionError, since the default limit is about 1000
Run in O(1) space, using the same stack frame
Be optimized by tail-call elimination in the interpreter
e:
Every recursive call adds a frame to the call stack. Python limits the depth to about 1000 frames by default to avoid crashing.
A path of 100,000 nodes needs 100,000 nested calls → RecursionError. Python does not optimize tail calls.
Fix: write it iteratively with your own stack (a list).
r: Deep recursion in Python → convert to a loop with a stack.
fa: Hit RecursionError (default limit ~1000)

q: Validate a string of brackets like `"([]{})"`. Data structure?
o: Queue
Stack
Heap
Trie
e:
A stack is last-in, first-out, like a pile of plates.
Walk through the string: push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; pop it. If it doesn't match, or the stack is empty, the string is invalid.
At the end the stack must be empty. O(n).
r: Matching pairs / nesting → stack.

q: Implementing a queue with two stacks gives what cost per operation?
o: O(n) each
O(1) amortized
O(log n)
O(n²) total
e:
Push new items onto stack `in`. To dequeue, pop from stack `out`; if `out` is empty, first move everything from `in` to `out`, which reverses the order so the oldest is on top.
A single move can be expensive, but each item is moved at most once in its life. Spread over all operations, the average cost is O(1): that is 'amortized' O(1).
r: Each item moves once → amortized O(1).

q: Autocomplete over a dictionary of words by prefix. Best structure?
o: A hash set of all the words
A trie (prefix tree)
A min-heap ordered by word length
A linked list of the words in order
e:
A trie is a tree where each edge is a letter. Words with the same beginning share the same path: 'car', 'cart' and 'care' all go through c → a → r.
To autocomplete 'ca', walk 2 steps down and collect all words below that node.
Lookup time depends on the prefix length, not on how many words are stored.
r: Prefix search → trie.
fa: Trie (prefix tree)

q: Count connected components while edges arrive dynamically. Best structure?
o: Union-Find with path compression and ranks
A stack that stores the vertices of each group
A binary search tree of all the vertices seen
A Bloom filter that stores the edges so far
e:
Union-Find keeps groups of elements. `find(x)` returns the group leader; `union(a, b)` merges two groups.
When an edge a-b arrives, union them; the number of components drops by one if they were in different groups.
With path compression and union by rank, each operation is almost O(1). Also used for Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.
r: Dynamic 'are these connected?' → Union-Find.
fa: Union-Find (disjoint set) with path compression and union by rank

q: Which traversal of a binary search tree yields keys in sorted order?
o: Pre-order
In-order
Post-order
Level-order
e:
In a BST, every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is bigger.
In-order traversal visits left subtree, then the node, then right subtree, so it naturally outputs keys from smallest to largest.
Pre-order (node first) is used to copy trees; post-order (node last) to delete them.
r: BST + in-order = sorted output.

q: Worst-case search time in an unbalanced BST built from sorted input?
o: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
e:
Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into a plain BST makes each new key the right child of the previous one. The 'tree' is really a straight line, like a linked list.
Searching then visits every node: O(n).
Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) reorganize themselves to keep height about log n, guaranteeing O(log n).
r: Unbalanced BST can degrade to O(n).

q: What does this function return and what are its time/space costs?
o: Smallest value; O(n log n) time, O(1) space
First duplicate value; O(n) time, O(n) space
Count of duplicates; O(n²) time, O(1) space
Last unique value; O(n) time, O(1) space
e:
It walks the list once and remembers each number in a set. The first number already in the set is the first repeated value, so it returns it.
One loop, with O(1) set checks inside: O(n) time. The set can grow to n items: O(n) extra memory.
Without the set you would compare every pair: O(n²).
r: A set turns 'have I seen it?' into O(1).

q: Space complexity of recursive DFS on a binary tree of height h?
o: O(1), since no extra memory is allocated
O(h) for the recursion call stack
O(n²), since each node is visited twice
O(log h) for the depth of the call stack
e:
Recursive DFS keeps one call-stack frame for each node on the current path from the root. The longest path has h nodes, so memory is O(h).
For a balanced tree h ≈ log n; for a completely skewed tree h = n.
BFS instead keeps a whole level in its queue: O(width).
r: Recursion memory = depth of the recursion.
fa: O(h) for the call stack

q: In a Python list, `append(x)` and `insert(0, x)` cost…
o: Both are O(1) in the average case
append: O(1) amortized; insert(0): O(n)
Both are O(n) since the list is copied
append: O(n); insert(0): O(1) in CPython
e:
A Python list is a dynamic array: items sit next to each other in memory.
Adding at the END just uses the next free slot: O(1) (occasionally the array grows, but on average still O(1)).
Inserting at the FRONT means shifting every existing item one place to the right: O(n). Use `collections.deque` if you need fast front inserts.
r: List end = fast. List front = slow.
fa: append O(1) amortized, insert(0, x) O(n)

q: Repeated `x in data` checks inside a loop are slow. `data` is a list of 1M items. Fix?
o: Sort the list once so the checks run faster
Build a `set` once, so each check is O(1)
Convert it to a tuple, which searches faster
Call `data.index(x)` for each of the checks
e:
`x in some_list` checks items one by one: O(n). Doing it inside a loop of n iterations costs O(n²), which is huge for a million items.
`x in some_set` uses hashing: O(1) on average.
Converting once costs O(n), then all checks are cheap.
r: Many membership checks → use a set.
fa: Convert to a `set` once, making each check O(1) average

q: Maximum subarray sum in O(n)?
o: Kadane's algorithm
Floyd-Warshall
Binary search
Merge sort
e:
Kadane's idea: walk through the array keeping `cur`, the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current position.
At each number x, either extend the previous subarray (`cur + x`) or start fresh at x, whichever is bigger. Track the best `cur` ever seen.
One pass, O(n) time, O(1) memory.
r: Kadane: extend or restart at each element.

q: Generating all permutations of n distinct elements takes at least…
o: O(n), because each element is visited once
O(n²), because each pair is compared
O(n!) outputs, and O(n · n!) to write them
O(2ⁿ), because each element is in or out
e:
There are n! orderings (3 items: 6; 10 items: 3,628,800), and each permutation has n elements to write out.
Such problems are solved with backtracking: choose an element, recurse on the rest, then undo the choice and try the next.
For comparison, the number of subsets is 2ⁿ.
r: Permutations = n!, subsets = 2ⁿ.
fa: O(n!) outputs, O(n · n!) to write them

q: For a sparse graph (E much smaller than V²), which representation is preferred?
o: Adjacency matrix
Adjacency list
Edge-weight matrix
Incidence matrix
e:
An adjacency list stores, for each node, only the list of its actual neighbors: O(V + E) memory. In Python: `{"A": ["B", "C"], ...}`.
An adjacency matrix is a V × V grid of yes/no, which wastes memory when most pairs are not connected, but checks 'is A connected to B?' in O(1).
Most real graphs (social networks, roads) are sparse.
r: Sparse graph → adjacency list.

q: Answer many `sum(nums[i:j])` range queries on a static array quickly?
o: Recompute each sum on demand, O(n) per query
Prefix sums: each query is `p[j] - p[i]`
Sort the array once, then slice the range
Keep a stack of partial sums for each query
e:
Build `prefix` where `prefix[k]` is the sum of the first k elements. This takes one pass.
Then the sum of any range i..j-1 is `prefix[j] - prefix[i]`: one subtraction.
For example nums = [3, 1, 4]: prefix = [0, 3, 4, 8]; sum of nums[1:3] = 8 - 3 = 5.
r: Many range sums → prefix sums.
fa: Precompute prefix sums once (O(n)); each query is `prefix[j] - prefix[i]` (O(1))

q: 'Next greater element' for each array item in O(n) uses…
o: A monotonic stack
A min-heap
Binary search on a sorted copy
A trie of the values
e:
Keep a stack of indexes whose next greater element is not known yet; their values are in decreasing order (that is why it is called 'monotonic').
When a new value is bigger than the top of the stack, it IS the answer for that item: pop it and record the answer. Repeat, then push the new index.
Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).
r: 'Next greater/smaller' → monotonic stack.

q: An LRU cache with O(1) get and put is typically built with…
o: A sorted list ordered by last use
A hash map plus a doubly linked list
A min-heap ordered by timestamp
Two stacks that swap their items
e:
LRU = Least Recently Used: when full, remove the item that was used longest ago.
The hash map finds any item in O(1). The doubly linked list keeps items in usage order: move an item to the front when used, remove from the back when full, both O(1).
In Python, `OrderedDict` (with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`) does exactly this.
r: LRU cache = hash map + doubly linked list.

q: For a positive integer n, what does `n & (n - 1) == 0` test?
o: n is an even number
n is a power of two
n is a prime number
n is an odd number
e:
In binary, a power of two has exactly one 1 bit: 8 = 1000. Subtracting 1 flips that bit and turns all lower bits into 1: 7 = 0111.
The AND (&) of 1000 and 0111 is 0000. Any number with two or more 1 bits keeps at least one, so the result is not 0.
The same trick `n & (n - 1)` removes the lowest 1 bit, which helps count bits.
r: n & (n-1) == 0 → power of two.

q: A dynamic array doubles capacity when full. Amortized cost of append?
o: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
e:
Most appends just use a free slot: O(1). When the array is full, it allocates double the space and copies everything: O(n) for that one append.
But copies happen only at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ... and they add up to less than 2n over n appends. Averaged over all appends, each costs O(1).
That average-over-many reasoning is called amortized analysis.
r: Rare expensive steps averaged over many cheap ones = amortized.

q: How do you approach a coding problem you have never seen in an interview?
a:
- Restate the problem; ask about input size, constraints and edge cases (empty input, duplicates, negatives).
- Work through 1-2 small examples by hand.
- Describe a brute-force solution and its complexity first.
- Look for patterns: hash map, two pointers, sliding window, sorting, heap, BFS/DFS, DP, binary search.
- Agree on the approach, then code cleanly with clear names, thinking aloud.
- Test with your examples and edge cases; trace the code line by line.
- State the final time and space complexity and possible improvements.

q: How does a hash map work internally?
a:
- An array of buckets. `hash(key) % capacity` chooses the bucket.
- Collisions (two keys, same bucket): chaining (a small list per bucket) or open addressing (try the next slots; Python dicts do this).
- When it gets too full (load factor), it resizes: a bigger array and every key re-placed. Amortized O(1) inserts.
- Keys must be hashable and must not change; equal keys must have equal hashes.
- Average O(1) get/put/delete; worst case O(n) with many collisions.

q: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively. Explain the pointers.
a:
- Keep `prev = None` and `curr = head`.
- Loop: save `nxt = curr.next`, point `curr.next = prev`, then move `prev = curr`, `curr = nxt`.
- When `curr` is None, `prev` is the new head.
- O(n) time, O(1) memory. A recursive version uses O(n) stack.
ac:
def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev, curr = curr, nxt
    return prev

q: What does Big-O notation describe?
o: The exact running time of a program in seconds
How time or memory grows as the input size grows
The size of the source code, measured in lines
The number of bugs a program has in total
e:
Big-O ignores machine speed and small details and answers: if the input becomes 10 times bigger, how much more work is needed?
- O(1): constant, same work for any size.
- O(log n): grows very slowly.
- O(n): grows in proportion.
- O(n²): 10× input → 100× work.
It usually describes the worst case.
r: Big-O = how cost grows with input size.
fa: How the running time (or memory) grows as the input size grows

q: What is the time complexity?
o: O(n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
e:
The loop runs once for each of the n items, and each iteration does a constant amount of work (one addition).
n iterations × constant work = O(n), called linear time: double the list, double the time.
r: One loop over n items = O(n).

q: What is the time complexity?
o: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2n)
e:
For each of the n items in the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times: n × n = n² iterations.
O(n²) is called quadratic: with 1,000 items that is about 1,000,000 checks; with 100,000 items, 10 billion.
A set can solve this specific problem in O(n).
r: Loop inside a loop over the same data = O(n²).

q: Accessing the 1000th element: array (Python list) vs linked list?
o: Both are O(1), since the position is known
Array: O(1); linked list: O(n), node by node
Array: O(n); linked list: O(1) with an index
Both are O(log n), halving the search space
e:
An array stores items next to each other in memory, so the position of item k can be calculated directly: O(1).
A linked list stores items in separate nodes, each pointing to the next. To reach item 1000 you must follow 1000 links: O(n).
In exchange, a linked list can insert or remove a node in O(1) once you are at the right place.
r: Array = fast access by index. Linked list = fast insert where you are.
fa: Array O(1); linked list O(n) because you must walk node by node

q: A stack is…
o: First in, first out (FIFO): the oldest leaves first
Last in, first out (LIFO): the newest leaves first
Kept sorted automatically as items are added
A kind of database used to hold temporary data
e:
Think of a pile of plates: you put a plate on top (push) and take the top one (pop). The last plate added is the first removed.
In Python a list works as a stack: `append()` to push, `pop()` to pop, both O(1).
Uses: undo history, matching brackets, the function call stack, DFS.
r: Stack = LIFO (pile of plates).
fa: Last in, first out (LIFO): you take from the top what you put last

q: A queue is…
o: Last in, first out (LIFO): the newest leaves first
First in, first out (FIFO): the oldest leaves first
Random order, with no rule for what is removed
A structure that stores only numbers, not text
e:
Like a line at the supermarket: people join at the back and are served from the front.
In Python use `collections.deque`: `append()` adds at the back, `popleft()` removes from the front, both O(1).
Uses: task queues, BFS, buffering messages.
r: Queue = FIFO (supermarket line).
fa: First in, first out (FIFO): the first item added is the first removed

q: Why must every recursive function have a base case?
c:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:          # base case
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)    # recursive case
o: It makes the function run faster on large inputs
Without it, the calls never stop (RecursionError)
Python requires it as part of the function syntax
It lets the function return a value to its caller
e:
Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem.
The base case is the simplest input that is answered directly, without another call (here n == 0). Each call must move closer to it.
Without a base case, the calls never stop and Python raises RecursionError when the call stack is too deep.
r: Recursion = base case + smaller recursive call.
fa: Without a condition that stops the recursion, the function calls itself forever (RecursionError)

q: Searching an unsorted list by checking each item one by one is…
o: O(1), since each item is checked once
O(log n), by halving the list
O(n): linear search
O(n²), by comparing every pair
e:
Linear search starts at the first item and compares each one until it finds the target or reaches the end. In the worst case it looks at all n items: O(n).
If the list were sorted you could use binary search (O(log n)); if you need many lookups, put the items in a set (O(1)).
r: Check every item = O(n).

q: In a tree data structure, what is a leaf?
o: The top node
A node with no children
Any node with two children
The connection between nodes
e:
A tree is made of nodes connected parent → child, with no cycles.
- Root: the single top node (no parent).
- Children: nodes directly below a node.
- Leaf: a node with no children.
- Height: number of levels from root to the deepest leaf.
Examples: folders on a disk, the HTML DOM, company org charts.
r: Root at the top, leaves at the bottom (no children).

q: What is a graph in computer science?
o: A chart with axes, used to plot data
A set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges
A sorted list of values with links
A type of loop that repeats over nodes
e:
A graph models things and connections between them: cities and roads, users and friendships, web pages and links.
Edges can be directed (one-way, like following someone) or undirected (two-way), and weighted (with a cost, like distance) or not.
A tree is a special graph with no cycles.
r: Graph = nodes + edges.

q: What must be true before you can use binary search on a list?
o: The list must have an even length
The list must be sorted
The list must contain only integers
The list must be smaller than 1000
e:
Binary search decides which half to discard by comparing the target with the middle element. That only makes sense if smaller values are on the left and bigger values on the right, i.e. the list is sorted.
On an unsorted list it gives wrong answers. If you search many times, sorting once (O(n log n)) then searching (O(log n) each) can pay off.
r: Binary search needs sorted data.

q: What is the time complexity of `nums[5]` on a Python list of 1 million items?
o: O(n)
O(log n)
e:
Lists are arrays, so the memory address of position 5 is calculated directly from where the list starts. It does not matter if the list has 10 or 10 million items.
That is constant time, written O(1). (O(5) is also 'constant', and Big-O drops constants, so we write O(1).)
r: Index access on a list = O(1).

q: What is an algorithm?
o: A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem
A programming language used to write programs
A type of database used to store records
A kind of computer chip used in servers
e:
An algorithm is a clear list of steps that always leads to a result. A cooking recipe is a good picture.
Example: 'find the largest number in a list' = look at each number and remember the biggest seen so far.
The same problem can have several algorithms; some are much faster than others, which is why we study complexity (Big-O).
r: Algorithm = a recipe for solving a problem.
fa: A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or doing a task

q: What is a data structure?
o: A way to organize data, like a list, set or tree
A building plan for the rooms of a server farm
A password that protects the data of a database
A type of error that the compiler can raise
e:
Data has to be arranged somehow in memory. Different arrangements make different operations fast or slow.
- List/array: access by position is fast.
- Dictionary (hash map): look up a value by key is fast.
- Set: check membership and keep unique values.
- Stack and queue: control the order in which items come out.
Choosing the right data structure is half of solving most interview problems.
r: Data structure = how data is organized in memory.
fa: A way of organizing and storing data so it can be used efficiently, such as a list, dictionary, set or tree

q: What is a dictionary (also called map or hash map)?
o: A set of key-value pairs, looked up by key
An ordered list of numbers, accessed by position
A text file that contains a list of words
A sorting algorithm that is used for text
e:
In a phone book you look up a name (key) and find a number (value). A dictionary works the same way.
Python: `ages = {"Ana": 30, "Luis": 25}` and `ages["Ana"]` returns 30. Java: `Map<String, Integer>` (`HashMap`).
Looking up a key takes about the same time no matter how big the dictionary is (O(1) on average).
r: Dictionary = key → value, fast lookup.
fa: A collection of key-value pairs where you look up a value by its key, like a phone book

q: What is special about a set?
o: Stores each value once; fast membership checks
It always keeps its values in sorted order
It can only store numbers, never text values
It allows duplicates and keeps their order
e:
A set is a collection with no duplicates. Adding the same value twice leaves one copy.
Python: `s = {1, 2, 2, 3}` becomes {1, 2, 3}. Java: `HashSet`.
It is the usual tool for removing duplicates and for fast membership checks (`x in s` is O(1) on average, while in a list it is O(n)).
r: Set = unique values + fast membership check.
fa: It stores each value only once and checks 'is this in the set?' very quickly

q: What is a 'brute force' solution?
o: A very fast and optimal solution to the problem
Trying every option: correct but often slow
A solution that needs special hardware to run
An attack that exists only in security work
e:
Brute force means the straightforward approach without clever tricks. Example: to find two numbers that add up to a target, check every pair with two nested loops (O(n²)).
In interviews, it is a good first step: state the brute force solution and its cost, then improve it (for example with a hash map in O(n)).
(In security, 'brute force' also names guessing passwords by trying many combinations.)
r: Brute force = try everything. Start there, then improve.
fa: Trying every possibility directly: simple and correct, but often too slow for big inputs

q: When we say an algorithm takes O(n) time, what is n?
o: The input size, like the number of items
The number of lines of code in the program
The number of CPU cores that the machine has
The number of programmers on the dev team
e:
Big-O describes how the work grows as the input grows. n is the input size.
O(n) means that if the list becomes 10 times longer, the work becomes about 10 times bigger.
O(n²) would be about 100 times bigger, and O(1) would stay the same.
r: n = size of the input.
fa: The size of the input, for example the number of items in the list

q: What is the difference between sorting and searching?
o: Sorting orders items; searching looks for one
They are the same operation under two names
Sorting deletes items; searching adds new ones
Searching only works on data that is sorted
e:
Sorting: [3, 1, 2] becomes [1, 2, 3].
Searching: is 2 in the list, and where? On an unsorted list you check items one by one (linear search, O(n)). On a sorted list you can use binary search (O(log n)).
This is why sorting first can pay off when you search many times.
r: Sorting orders. Searching finds.
fa: Sorting puts the items in a defined order; searching finds a particular item (or checks if it exists)
